etymology: Adam Johns's longtime call sign and family/Marine Corps nickname; carried into ministry as the working identity of U.S.M.C. Ministries (Under Strict Marching Christ-ward) and stamped on this dictionary as the editor's mark. Not a biblical word; included here as the editor's own easter egg in the dictionary that bears his name.
biblical_def: MOOP is the call sign Adam Johns has gone by since young manhood — a nickname that followed him through the Marine Corps, into marriage, into fatherhood, and into the ministry work that produced this dictionary. The four letters are not an acronym but a name, the way "Pip" is a name in Dickens or "Aslan" is a name in Lewis. The biblical principle behind the inclusion of a personal name in a personal dictionary is the principle of Genesis 2:19-20 — God brought every creature to Adam to see what HE would call it, and "whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof." The Adam who edits this dictionary stands in the long line of namers, and as a namer he is named himself. This entry is the editor's signature in the wall of the work — the way medieval craftsmen carved their initials into the cathedral stones they shaped. It is not Scripture; it is the mark of the man whose hands shaped these pages. The whole project is dedicated to the glory of the One True Name; this small entry simply acknowledges who held the pen.
webster_summary: Adam Johns's lifelong nickname; the editor's signature in his own dictionary; not biblical but humanly real.
webster_full: MOOP, name. The nickname / call sign of Adam Johns, founder of U.S.M.C. Ministries and editor of this dictionary. Carries no formal biblical sense; included as the editor's personal mark.
Like a stonemason's chisel-mark in a cathedral wall, this entry signs the work: a man with a real name shaped these pages by the grace of God.
scriptures: Genesis 2:19-20

And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field.
Revelation 2:17
To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.
Isaiah 62:2
And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all kings thy glory: and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the LORD shall name thee.
Philippians 4:3
And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life.
corruption_summary: There is no corruption to flag for a personal nickname; what can be said is that the editor's earnest desire is that this dictionary serve Christ and not the editor — the name MOOP appears once, in this entry, as acknowledgment of authorship; everywhere else the name on the lips is Jesus.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation in editing a personal-name dictionary is to make it about the editor rather than about the Christ the dictionary serves. Every page of this work that names a doctrine, a person, or a passage is intended to point past the editor to the One the editor seeks to glorify. The MOOP entry exists in the dictionary the way an author's name appears on the spine of a book — once, to signify authorship; and then the book itself takes over.

Adam's deeper hope is that on the last day his white stone (Rev 2:17) will have a NEW NAME written on it, the name that no man knows but he that receiveth it. Whatever MOOP has meant in this life — call sign, husband, father, Marine, editor, brother — the name God will give in glory will be sweeter and more fitting than every nickname this world has assigned. Until then: MOOP is the working signature on this wall.
roots_summary: MOOP is a personal nickname with no formal etymological derivation; it is a sound the family and the corps used until it became a name; included here as the editor's stonemason-mark.
roots_lines: Origin: Adam Johns's lifelong call sign / family nickname, carried through the Marine Corps and into ministry
Biblical principle: every namer is also named; the editor of a dictionary inevitably leaves his signature in it (Gen 2:19-20)
Functional: the editor's signature mark in his own work, the way medieval craftsmen carved initials into cathedral stones
Eschatological: every earthly name yields to the new name God will write on the white stone (Rev 2:17) of the overcomer
usage: MOOP is the editor's mark in the dictionary's wall — one stonemason's chisel-cut among many.
When God renames His people in glory, He will assign a name sweeter than every nickname this world has given.
Whatever the editor has been called in this life, the dictionary's purpose is to lift up the One Name above every name (Phil 2:9-11).

etymology: From Hebrew Miryam (H4813), the same root as Mary, Miriam, Marah, and Maria; root meaning is associated with marah (bitter) — the bitter waters Moses healed at Marah (Exod 15:23-25) where God demonstrated that what is bitter to nature can be made sweet by the Cross-tree thrown into the waters. The Spanish/Italian/Latin variant of the biblical Miriam/Mary.
biblical_def: Maria is the romance-language form of the great biblical name Miryam (Miriam / Mary), and it shares the same root: a Hebrew word-family whose surface meaning is BITTER. Moses's sister Miriam was named bitter; the place of the bitter waters in the wilderness was Marah ("bitter," Exod 15:23). And then — at Marah — God taught Moses the most precious wilderness lesson: He showed Moses A TREE, and when Moses threw the tree into the bitter waters, the waters were made sweet (Exod 15:25). The water did not change its source; the tree changed what flowed out of it. A bitter name does not have to remain a bitter life when the Tree — the Cross-tree of Jesus Christ — is cast into it. The wife of the editor of this dictionary bears the name Maria, and through her the meaning of the name has been made personally true: a woman named for bitterness has been transformed by the Holy Spirit into a woman of sweetness, hospitality, prayer, courage in mothering, and faithfulness in long obedience. The tree thrown into her life was the cross of Christ; the Spirit who indwells her is the water made sweet. "His countenance was as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars. His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely" (Song 5:15-16). The woman who in Hebrew is BITTER becomes in Christ ALTOGETHER LOVELY. This is the Marah miracle made personal.
webster_summary: The Latin/Spanish/Italian form of Hebrew Miriam/Mary; same root as Marah (bitter); the dictionary editor's wife, sweetened by the Cross-tree thrown into the bitter waters.
webster_full: MARIA, personal name. The Latin / Spanish / Italian variant of biblical Hebrew Miryam (Mary, Miriam). Root associated with bitterness (Hebrew marah) — the bitter waters of Exodus 15:23-25.

The wife of the editor of this dictionary bears this name; the biblical story of Marah — where God showed Moses the Tree to throw into the bitter waters and make them sweet — is her testimony in miniature. The bitter name has been made sweet by the Cross-tree and the indwelling Holy Spirit.
scriptures: Exodus 15:23-25

And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet.
Song of Solomon 5:16
His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
Galatians 5:22-23
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.
Proverbs 31:30-31
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.
corruption_summary: Maria the name is sometimes confused with the Marian dogmas of Rome (Immaculate Conception, Assumption, Mediatrix) — these are NOT taught by Scripture and are not part of the meaning of the name; Mary the mother of Christ was blessed (Luke 1:28, 42) but not co-mediatrix; this entry is about a specific woman bearing the name, not the Marian theological errors.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman Mariology has built around the name an enormous superstructure of doctrines unknown to the apostolic faith: the Immaculate Conception (1854), the Assumption (1950), Mary as Co-Redemptrix / Mediatrix of All Graces, the Marian apparitions of Lourdes and Fatima, the Rosary as devotional center. None of this is in Scripture; the canonical Mary said "Be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38), magnified the Lord (Luke 1:46-55), pondered things in her heart (Luke 2:19), and stood under her son's cross (John 19:25). She is BLESSED — uniquely so — but she is not co-mediatrix. There is one Mediator (1 Tim 2:5).

Maria the name as borne by ordinary Christian women through history has been a name of dignity, of motherhood, of faithful endurance. The wife who bears it in this household has lived its sweetness daily — and the editor of this dictionary is daily grateful that the Lord chose this Maria for him. The bitter root of the name has not been her experience; the Cross-tree cast in early made the waters sweet long ago, and the Holy Spirit has kept them sweet ever since. The honor of her life is real, and it is the Lord's doing through her.
roots_summary: Hebrew Miryam (H4813) — Maria/Mary/Miriam; shares root with marah (bitter, H4751); the Cross-tree of Marah turns the bitter waters sweet (Exod 15:25).
roots_lines: Hebrew Miryam (H4813) — the proper name; Maria, Mary, Miriam, Marah all share the root
Hebrew marah (H4751) — bitter; the surface meaning of the name's root
Exodus 15:23-25 — at the bitter waters of Marah, God showed Moses a TREE to cast in; the waters were made sweet
Typology: the Cross-tree (Christ crucified) cast into a bitter name / a bitter life turns the waters sweet by the indwelling Spirit
usage: A name that means bitter does not have to remain a bitter life when the Cross-tree is cast into it.
The wife who bears this name has lived the Marah miracle — sweetened by the Tree and kept sweet by the Spirit.
Maria the name carries the Hebrew Miryam root; the woman who bears it bears the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22-23).

etymology: Hebrew Marah (H4785) — "bitter" or "bitterness"; the place in the wilderness of Shur, three days' journey from the Red Sea, where Israel found water but could not drink it because it was bitter (Exod 15:23). God showed Moses a TREE to cast into the waters; the waters were made sweet.
biblical_def: Marah is the place-name and event in Exodus 15:22-26 where Israel — three days from the Red Sea, parched and complaining — found water at last only to discover it was bitter and undrinkable. The Hebrew marah means "bitter" or "bitterness"; the same root underlies the names Mary, Miriam, Maria, and Naomi's grief-cry (Ruth 1:20 — "call me not Naomi, call me Mara"). At Marah, the people murmured: "What shall we drink?" Moses cried to the LORD; and the LORD SHOWED HIM A TREE — Hebrew 'ets — which when Moses cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet. The text immediately adds: "There he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them, And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee." (Exod 15:25-26). Marah is therefore the place where God reveals Himself as YAHWEH-RAPHA — "the LORD that healeth thee" (Jehovah-Rapha). The typology is rich: the bitter waters picture human nature, embittered by the Fall and undrinkable for thirst; the Tree cast into them pictures the Cross of Christ — "who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree" (1 Pet 2:24). The Tree cast into the bitter waters made them sweet; the Cross cast into bitter humanity made redemption available. The Marah place became a place of HEALING because God showed Moses a tree.
webster_summary: The bitter waters in the wilderness made sweet when Moses cast in the Tree God showed him; type of the Cross of Christ cast into bitter humanity to heal it.
webster_full: MARAH, noun. (1) Place name in the wilderness of Shur (Exod 15:23-26) — the bitter waters that Moses healed by casting in the Tree God showed him. (2) Hebrew word for "bitter" / "bitterness" — root of the names Mary, Miriam, Maria, and Naomi's grief-name (Ruth 1:20).
Typology: the Cross of Christ (the Tree, 1 Pet 2:24; Gal 3:13) cast into the bitter waters of human nature; God reveals Himself there as Jehovah-Rapha, the LORD that healeth thee.
scriptures: Exodus 15:23-26

And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah... And the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet... I am the LORD that healeth thee.
1 Peter 2:24
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
Galatians 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.
Ruth 1:20
And she said unto them, Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.
corruption_summary: Marah is corrupted when the place is treated as a mere geographic note in the Exodus itinerary, or when the Tree-of-Marah typology is severed from the Cross of Christ; the Spirit-given Exodus 15 link to Yahweh-Rapha and the NT "on the tree" language (1 Pet 2:24; Gal 3:13) are deliberate.
corruption_paragraphs: Itinerary-only reading. Modernist commentary sometimes treats Marah as a stop on the Exodus map without theological weight — Israel was thirsty, Moses found a remedy, story moves on. But the canonical text immediately attaches a covenant statute ("if thou wilt diligently hearken") and a divine self-revelation ("I am the LORD that healeth thee" — Jehovah-Rapha). Marah is one of the great Jehovah-name revelation events of the OT, paralleling Jehovah-Jireh (Gen 22) and Jehovah-Nissi (Exod 17:15). To strip it of weight is to lose a Name of God.

Tree-typology severance. The detail that God SHOWED MOSES A TREE which when cast into the bitter waters healed them is theologically loaded. 1 Peter 2:24 and Galatians 3:13 both use "on the tree" language for the Cross of Christ. The Spirit's choice of "tree" rather than "piece of wood" or "branch" in Exod 15:25 invites the typological reading: the Cross-tree, cast into the bitter waters of human nature, makes them sweet. To dismiss this as fanciful is to miss the deliberate canonical pattern.
roots_summary: Hebrew Marah (H4785) — bitter; the place where God showed Moses a Tree to heal the bitter waters (Exod 15:23-26); Yahweh-Rapha revealed.
roots_lines: Hebrew Marah (H4785) — bitter, bitterness; the place name (Exod 15:23)
Hebrew marah (H4751) — bitter; root of Mary, Miriam, Maria, Mara (Naomi's grief-cry, Ruth 1:20)
Hebrew 'ets — tree; the Tree God showed Moses to cast into the waters (Exod 15:25); same word the NT uses for the Cross (1 Pet 2:24; Gal 3:13)
Yahweh-Rapha — "the LORD that healeth thee" — God's self-revelation at Marah after the bitter waters are made sweet (Exod 15:26)
usage: The Tree God showed Moses, cast into the bitter waters, made them sweet — type of the Cross cast into bitter humanity.
At Marah God revealed Himself as Jehovah-Rapha — the LORD that healeth thee — the first healing-name of God.
What Marah, Maria, Mary, Miriam, and Mara all share is a Hebrew root for bitterness — and a Tree that can change the taste of the water.

etymology: Hebrew Mal'akhi (H4401) — "my messenger" or "messenger of Yahweh" (the name of the last book of the OT); paired with Greek Andreas (G406) — "manly" or "brave" (the name of the apostle Andrew, Peter's brother). Personal memorial entry for the first child of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2017 in Okinawa, Japan, before he could be born and named publicly.
biblical_def: Malachi Andrew is the name Adam and Maria Johns prepared for their first child, whom they lost to miscarriage in 2017 while stationed in Okinawa, Japan. The name brought together two great biblical figures: MALACHI ("my messenger"), the prophet who closed the Old Testament with the promise that the messenger of the covenant would come (Mal 3:1) and that the Sun of Righteousness would arise with healing in His wings (Mal 4:2) — the last word of God before 400 silent years and the dawn of Christ; and ANDREW (Greek Andreas, "manly" or "courageous"), the disciple who FIRST brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:40-42), the patron of those who bring others to Christ. The name itself was a prayer: that this son would be a messenger, manly and courageous, bringing others to the Sun of Righteousness. The Lord's providence did not give this little boy a public life on this earth — but the biblical hope of Christian parents reaches further than the wombs that hold their children. "David... fasted, and went in, and lay all night upon the earth" while the child was sick; but when the child died, David rose, washed, anointed himself, and worshipped, saying, "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me" (2 Sam 12:23). The covenant promise is sure: the children of believers belong to the LORD; the little ones taken from us before they were named in the world are named in heaven. Malachi Andrew is known by his name to his parents and to the Lord who keeps the unborn (Ps 139:13-16). This entry is dedicated to his memory and to the day Adam and Maria shall see him, in the resurrection-morning of the Sun of Righteousness whose name his name carried.
webster_summary: Memorial entry for the first child of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2017 in Okinawa, Japan; named for the prophet Malachi ("messenger") and the apostle Andrew ("manly"); known by his name to the Lord.
webster_full: MALACHI ANDREW, memorial entry. The name given by Adam and Maria Johns to their first child, lost to miscarriage in 2017 in Okinawa, Japan.

Combines two biblical names: Malachi ("my messenger" — the prophet of the last OT book, herald of the Sun of Righteousness) and Andrew ("manly" — the apostle who first brought Peter to Jesus). A prayer-name for a son who was loved before he was named.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 12:22-23

And he said, While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept: for I said, Who can tell whether GOD will be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.

For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well. My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth. Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Malachi 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Matthew 18:10
Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: There is no corruption to expose for a memorial; what can be said is that modernist medical / secular culture often presses grieving parents to treat unborn children as not-yet-persons; the Scriptures (Ps 139; Jer 1:5; Luke 1:41-44) treat them as fully-known persons whose names are known to God before they are spoken aloud.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern secular medical culture often counsels parents after miscarriage to think of the lost child as merely "tissue," "a cluster of cells," or "not yet really a baby." This is a profound dehumanization of the unborn. The canonical text is explicit: David fasted and wept while his infant was DYING and rose to worship after the child DIED, acknowledging him as a real person whom David would JOIN one day (2 Sam 12:23). The unborn John the Baptist leaped for joy in Elisabeth's womb (Luke 1:41) — joy is a person's response. Jeremiah was known before he was formed in the womb (Jer 1:5). Christian parents grieving miscarriage are grieving the loss of a known person, not of mere tissue, and their grief is dignified by Scripture.

The pastoral side of this is the Reformed covenant promise. "For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the LORD our God shall call" (Acts 2:39). Children of believing parents, including those who die before public confession, are received under God's covenant care; the historic Reformed confessions (e.g., WCF 10.3) explicitly confess that elect infants dying in infancy are saved through Christ. The grief of losing a Malachi Andrew is real; the hope of seeing him again is also real, and it rests on the same Christ whose name Malachi's name was meant to herald.

I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me — David's word after losing his infant son is the Christian parent's hope after miscarriage.
The Sun of Righteousness whose name Malachi's name carried will rise on the resurrection morning and gather all His little ones home.

etymology: English "hope," rendering Greek elpis (G1680) and Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — confident expectation of God's promised good. Personal memorial entry for one of two twin daughters of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan, alongside her sister Mercy.
biblical_def: Hope is the name Adam and Maria Johns gave to one of their two twin daughters lost to miscarriage in 2018, while stationed in Okinawa, Japan. The name was given in the same Spirit that gave her sister's name — MERCY: two daughters together, two virtues paired, the heart of the Christian gospel in two little names. Hope in biblical theology is not wish or optimism but CONFIDENT EXPECTATION of God's promised good (Rom 8:24-25; Heb 11:1; 1 Pet 1:3 — "a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead"). The Christian who names a daughter Hope is making a sermon out of her name: that this child will live in the certain expectation of the resurrection, the new heavens, the coming Lord. Hope and her sister Mercy never drew earthly breath, but the name remains a confession: their parents named them in the hope that one day they will hold them again. "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity" (1 Cor 13:13) — Hope is part of the triad that endures into the resurrection-morning. The name carries no shadow of disappointment; the canonical word is BLESSED ARE THEY THAT MOURN, FOR THEY SHALL BE COMFORTED (Matt 5:4). This memorial entry stands as Hope's name in the Johns family dictionary — a name borne by a daughter known to her parents and to God, whose face her parents long to see in the morning of the resurrection.
webster_summary: Memorial entry for one of two twin daughters of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa; named with her sister Mercy for the two virtues that endure into the resurrection.
webster_full: HOPE (TWIN), memorial entry. The name given by Adam and Maria Johns to one of two twin daughters lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan. The other twin was named Mercy.
The biblical virtue of confident expectation in God's promised good (Rom 8:24-25; Heb 11:1; 1 Pet 1:3); paired with her sister Mercy as a two-name confession of the gospel heart.
scriptures: 1 Peter 1:3
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.
Romans 8:24-25
For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.
Hebrews 11:1
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
1 Corinthians 13:13
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
corruption_summary: There is no corruption to flag for a child's memorial; the corruption to flag is the cultural reduction of hope from confident expectation of God's promised good to mere optimism or wish — the biblical word carries weight that modern usage has nearly emptied.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern English has flattened "hope" into "wishful thinking" — "I hope it doesn't rain." The biblical Greek elpis is something different and stronger: confident expectation grounded in the character of God who has promised. Romans 8:24-25 distinguishes hope-for-what-is-not-seen from hope-for-what-is-already-visible: biblical hope is necessarily for what is NOT YET seen, but is CERTAIN because of who promised. The daughter named Hope was not given a wish-name; she was given a certainty-name.

Christian parents who lose children before they are born have a specific application of biblical hope: their hope is not that the child will somehow return to them in this life (David's word in 2 Sam 12:23 forbids that hope), but that they will go TO the child in the resurrection-morning, where every tear is wiped from every eye (Rev 21:4). The hope is forward, not backward; it is rooted in the resurrection of Christ; it is held with patience while waiting (Rom 8:25). This is the hope Hope's name confesses, and it is the hope Adam and Maria carry forward.

Paired with her sister Mercy: a two-name confession of the gospel's heart — hope and mercy together endure into the resurrection
usage: Hope is not a wish; it is the certain expectation of what God has promised — the name Adam and Maria gave their first twin daughter.
We are saved by hope — and hope that is seen is not hope, but hope unseen we wait for with patience.
Hope and her sister Mercy were named together; together they wait in the morning of the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

etymology: Old French merci, from Latin merces (reward, wages, payment); rendering Greek eleos (G1656) — compassion, pity, kindness in the face of misery; and Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness. Personal memorial entry for one of two twin daughters of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan, alongside her sister Hope.
biblical_def: Mercy is the name Adam and Maria Johns gave to one of their two twin daughters lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan. She was named alongside her sister HOPE — two virtues paired, two daughters named together, the heart of the Christian gospel in two little names. Mercy in biblical theology is COMPASSION TOWARD THE MISERABLE — God's free disposition to alleviate the suffering He could justly leave in place. Greek eleos (G1656) is the disposition; Hebrew chesed (H2617) is the covenant lovingkindness that does what justice did not require. "His mercy endureth for ever" (Ps 136 — repeated 26 times in one psalm); "his mercies are new every morning" (Lam 3:22-23). The Beatitudes promise "blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Matt 5:7), and Paul opens the great mercy-discourse of Romans with "I beseech you therefore, brethren, BY THE MERCIES OF GOD" (Rom 12:1). The daughter named Mercy was given a name that points back to the Father of Mercies (2 Cor 1:3) and forward to the eternal mercy that endures forever. With her sister Hope she completes a two-name confession: mercy is the ground of our salvation (Eph 2:4-5 — "God, who is rich in mercy"), and hope is the certainty of our reception of it (1 Pet 1:3). This memorial entry stands as Mercy's name in the Johns family dictionary — a name borne by a daughter known to her parents and to the Father of Mercies who receives the little ones.
webster_summary: Memorial entry for one of two twin daughters of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa; named with her sister Hope for the two virtues that endure into the resurrection.
webster_full: MERCY (TWIN), memorial entry. The name given by Adam and Maria Johns to one of two twin daughters lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan. The other twin was named Hope.
Greek eleos (G1656) — compassion toward the miserable; Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness. Paired with her sister Hope as a two-name confession of the gospel's heart.
scriptures: Ephesians 2:4-5
But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved.)
Lamentations 3:22-23
It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
Matthew 5:7
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
1 Peter 2:10
Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.
corruption_summary: There is no corruption to flag for a child's memorial; the corruption to flag is the modern cultural emptying of mercy from a covenantal, theologically dense reality into sentimental tolerance or therapeutic non-judgmentalism.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture often substitutes "tolerance" or "non-judgmentalism" for the biblical reality of mercy. But mercy in Scripture presupposes WRATH RIGHTLY DESERVED. "God, who is rich in mercy, FOR HIS GREAT LOVE WHEREWITH HE LOVED US, EVEN WHEN WE WERE DEAD IN SINS" (Eph 2:4-5). Mercy without the underlying judgment is sentimentality, not grace. The God of mercy is the God who would have been just to leave us in the death of sin — and chose instead, in Christ, to give us life. The daughter named Mercy was given a name laden with covenant theology, not just kindness.

Christian parents losing children before they are born live in the daily reception of mercy. The hope that the lost children are received by the Father of Mercies is itself mercy received. The strength to keep walking after such losses is mercy received. The marriage that survives such losses, the faith that holds through the dark mornings, the work that continues to bear fruit — all are mercies of God, new every morning (Lam 3:22-23). Mercy the daughter has a mother and father whose own lives have been kept by mercies they did not earn; her name speaks of what kept them, and what now keeps her.
roots_summary: Greek eleos (G1656), Hebrew chesed (H2617) — compassion toward the miserable; covenant lovingkindness; memorial entry for Mercy, twin daughter of Adam and Maria Johns lost in 2018 in Okinawa.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness, steadfast love; "his mercy endureth for ever" (Ps 136)
Personal: one of two twin daughters of Adam and Maria Johns, lost to miscarriage in 2018 in Okinawa, Japan
Paired with her sister Hope: a two-name confession of the gospel — mercy is the ground, hope is the certainty
usage: Mercy is compassion in the face of misery rightly deserving judgment; it is the gospel's ground.
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy — the Beatitude that turned a daughter's name into a sermon.
Mercy and her sister Hope were named together; together they wait in the morning of the great mercy that endures forever.

etymology: Modern English compound name — "Lu" (from Louise, Louisa, or Lucia — light, fame in battle) + "Anne" (from Hebrew Hannah, H2584, meaning "grace" or "favor"). Not biblical in itself but built from the biblical Hannah-grace root in the second element.
biblical_def: Luanne is a modern English compound name pairing "Lu" (a shortened form of Louise, Louisa, or Lucia — each carrying senses of light or famed-in-battle) with "Anne" (a Western European form of Hebrew Hannah, H2584 — grace, favor). Though Luanne is not itself a biblical name, the second element carries the great biblical root chanan (to be gracious) that runs from Hannah the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 1-2) through every Anne, Ann, Anna, Hannah, Joanna, John, and John-Baptizer in the canon. Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2 is one of the great female-voiced theological songs of the OT, foreshadowing Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55): "My heart rejoiceth in the LORD, mine horn is exalted in the LORD; my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies; because I rejoice in thy salvation" (1 Sam 2:1). This entry is dedicated personally to LUANNE JOHNS, the mother of Adam Johns and grandmother of the children mentioned elsewhere in this dictionary (Gideon, Boaz, Shiloh, and the three little ones taken too soon). Her name was not chosen for biblical etymology, but it carries the Hannah-grace inside it; and her life as wife, mother, and grandmother has lived out the grace that the Hannah-root quietly preaches. The dictionary thanks her with this entry.
webster_summary: Modern English compound name combining "Lu" (light/famed-in-battle) and "Anne" (Hebrew Hannah, grace); personal entry dedicated to Luanne Johns, mother of the editor.
webster_full: LUANNE, personal name (feminine). A modern English compound combining "Lu" (Louise, Louisa, Lucia) and "Anne" (from Hebrew Hannah, H2584 — grace).
Not itself a biblical name; carries the Hannah-grace root in its second element. Personally dedicated to Luanne Johns, mother of the editor of this dictionary.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 2:1
And Hannah prayed, and said, My heart rejoiceth in the LORD, mine horn is exalted in the LORD; my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies; because I rejoice in thy salvation.
Proverbs 31:28
Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, he praiseth her.
Proverbs 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Ephesians 6:2-3
Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth.
corruption_summary: There is no theological corruption to expose for a personal name; what may be added is that the dignity of motherhood and grandmotherhood — categories the editor's mother has lived in for decades — is one of the most fundamental created goods, increasingly devalued in modern secular culture and worth specific honor here.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern secular culture has progressively devalued the vocation of motherhood — treating it as one option among many, often as the lesser option compared to career, achievement, or self-actualization. The Bible takes the opposite view: motherhood is the FIRST blessing God spoke over the new couple in Eden (Gen 1:28), the FIRST hope of the post-Fall promise (Gen 3:15 — the woman's seed), and the deep dignity of every Hannah, Sarah, Elizabeth, Mary, and Lois (Timothy's grandmother, 2 Tim 1:5). The grandmother who has poured her years into raising children and supporting her children's children has lived the deepest current of Scripture.

Adam's mother Luanne has been one of the consistent presences in his life through Marine Corps deployments, the births of three living grandchildren, and the losses of three unborn grandchildren. Her name in this dictionary is a small act of honor (Eph 6:2-3) from a son who has been loved by her. The honor of mothers is the first command with promise; the editor names his mother here because she has earned the honor by living it.

The grandmother who has poured years into raising children and grandchildren has lived the deepest current of Scripture.

etymology: Old Norse Rögnvaldr — "ruler's counsel" or "mighty ruler," from regin (counsel, decision, power) + valdr (ruler). A Scottish/Scandinavian name brought into English through the Highlands; not itself biblical but carrying the same root-concepts as the biblical "counsellor" titles (Isa 9:6 — "Wonderful, Counsellor") and the biblical category of righteous rule.
biblical_def: Ronald is an Old Norse name meaning "ruler's counsel" or "mighty ruler," from the elements regin (counsel, divine decree) and valdr (ruler). Though not itself a biblical name, the elements it carries are biblical categories: COUNSEL (the wisdom-of-rule, as in the Wonderful COUNSELLOR title of the Messiah, Isa 9:6) and RULE (the kingly-prerogative responsibility, as in Romans 13's good ruler). This entry is dedicated personally to RONALD JOHNS, the brother of the editor — one of the family men whose names appear in this dictionary because every dictionary of a man's heart eventually includes the names of his brothers. The biblical category of brotherhood is high — "a brother is born for adversity" (Prov 17:17), "a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Prov 18:24), and the deep love between David and Jonathan, between Aaron and Moses, between James and John. Brothers in Scripture are sometimes rivals (Cain and Abel; Jacob and Esau; Joseph's brothers) and sometimes faithful companions (Aaron-Moses; James-John; the apostles together). The brother named Ronald has been part of the long thread of family life that produced the editor and continues to shape the work. The name was not chosen for biblical reasons, but the man bearing it stands inside biblical categories — son, brother, family, the long covenant lines of one family's history under God's providence.
webster_summary: Old Norse name meaning "ruler's counsel" or "mighty ruler"; not biblical itself but carrying the canonical categories of counsel and rule; personally dedicated to Ronald Johns, brother of the editor.

scriptures: Proverbs 17:17
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Proverbs 18:24
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Psalm 133:1
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
corruption_summary: There is no theological corruption to expose for a personal name; what may be added is that the modern devaluing of family relationships — especially adult sibling bonds — runs counter to the biblical pattern where brothers are part of a person's lifelong covenant community.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern American culture has tended to atomize the family — children leave home, scatter across the country for jobs, and adult sibling relationships often dwindle to holiday phone calls. The Bible presents a different pattern. Brothers in Scripture remain part of each other's lives across decades; their names appear in each other's stories; their support in adversity (Prov 17:17) is reckoned a real and continuing thing. Ronald Johns is named here because the editor's brothers are part of his life's covenant community, not just historical relatives.

The biblical category of brotherhood is also a typological resource. "For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). Christ Himself becomes the elder brother of every believer, not ashamed to call us brethren. Earthly brotherhood is a small picture of the family of God; thanking God for one's brothers prepares the heart to thank God for the Brother who is Christ.

etymology: Surname Johns — patronymic from "John" (Hebrew Yochanan through Greek Iōannēs, G2491), meaning "Yahweh is gracious." The family that produced the editor of this dictionary carries in its surname the same root that names John the Baptist, John the Apostle, and the line of Christian Johns through history.
biblical_def: The surname JOHNS is the patronymic English form of the great biblical name John — Hebrew Yochanan through Greek Iōannēs — meaning "Yahweh is gracious." Two of the most important figures in the NT carry this name: JOHN THE BAPTIST, the forerunner of Christ in the Spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:13-17); and JOHN THE APOSTLE, son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved, author of the fourth Gospel, the three Johannine epistles, and Revelation. The surname Johns therefore carries the root of "the LORD is gracious" in its etymology, and the family that bears it is privileged to wear that confession daily without saying a word. This entry is the EDITOR'S DEDICATION of the MOOP Dictionary to the Johns family — to Adam (the editor) and Maria (his wife); to their three living children Gideon, Boaz, and Shiloh; to their three little ones taken before they could be held — Malachi Andrew (2017), Hope and Mercy (twins, 2018) — all lost during Adam's military service in Okinawa, Japan; to Adam's mother Luanne and his brothers David, Joshua, and Ronald and his sister Hannah; to grandparents, in-laws, and the wider clan that produced him. The dictionary is not for the Johns family alone — it is for the wider church and any seeking soul who reads it — but its existence rests on the long covenant providence of God toward this particular family. Every dictionary has a dedication; this is mine.
webster_summary: Editor's dedication of the MOOP Dictionary to the Johns family — Adam and Maria; their three living children and three lost in Okinawa; Adam's mother, brothers, and sister; the long covenant providence that made the work possible.
webster_full: JOHNS FAMILY, dedication entry. The surname Johns is the patronymic English form of biblical John (Yochanan, Iōannēs) — "Yahweh is gracious."

This entry dedicates the MOOP Dictionary to the family of the editor: Adam and Maria; the living children Gideon, Boaz, and Shiloh; the three lost in Okinawa (Malachi Andrew 2017, Hope and Mercy 2018); Adam's mother Luanne and his brothers David, Joshua, and Ronald, and his sister Hannah.
scriptures: Joshua 24:15

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Psalm 127:3-5

Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of a youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them.
Deuteronomy 7:9
Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations.
Acts 2:39
For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the LORD our God shall call.
corruption_summary: There is no corruption to expose for a family dedication; what may be added is that modern atomized individualism often denies the biblical reality of family covenant lines — God's promises run through families, generations, and clan-stories, not just through individuals.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern theology, especially in evangelical traditions that emphasize personal-decision conversion, has sometimes underplayed the COVENANTAL FAMILY dimension of the Christian faith. But the Reformed tradition has always confessed that "the promise is unto you, AND TO YOUR CHILDREN" (Acts 2:39); that God keeps covenant mercy "to a thousand generations" (Deut 7:9); that children are an inheritance from the LORD (Ps 127:3); and that the household-faith of Joshua 24:15 — "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" — is a covenant pattern, not just an individualistic preference. The Johns family, like every Christian household, lives inside this covenant pattern.

The reason for the family dedication is not pride but gratitude. The editor of this dictionary did not produce the work alone; he was made possible by his parents, supported by his wife, encouraged by his children, prayed for by his siblings, and held by the long-faithful providence of God toward his family across generations. To dedicate the work to the family is simply to acknowledge what is so. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights" (James 1:17). The Johns family is one of those good gifts in the editor's life, and the dictionary now bears their name in its pages as one act of thanks.

etymology: Japanese Okinawa — "rope in the open sea," a chain of islands south of mainland Japan; major Marine Corps duty station for U.S. forces in the Pacific. Personal entry: the place where Adam Johns served as a Marine and where his family experienced both joy and the deep loss of three unborn children (Malachi Andrew, 2017; Hope and Mercy, 2018).
biblical_def: Okinawa is a chain of Japanese islands south of the mainland — the southernmost prefecture of Japan, a Pacific outpost where U.S. Marine Corps forces have long been stationed. The name in Japanese means "rope in the open sea," suggesting a long thin string of islands trailing into the Pacific. For the editor of this dictionary, Okinawa is not just a geographic location but a personal place of formation and loss. It was during military service in Okinawa that Adam and Maria Johns walked through two miscarriages — their first child Malachi Andrew (2017) and their twin daughters Hope and Mercy (2018). The place therefore carries in their family memory the texture of a biblical "place of grief" — like RAMAH (where "Rachel weeping for her children, refused to be comforted, because they are not," Jer 31:15; Matt 2:18), or BETHEL (Gen 35:8 — Deborah's burial place "under an oak," called Allon-bachuth, "oak of weeping"), or GETHSEMANE (where Christ Himself prayed in agony). The Bible names places of grief and gives them weight; the family that loses children in a specific geography carries that geography forever as part of the story God is writing for them. Okinawa is in the Johns family story not because the loss defines the place, but because the place will always remember the loss — and so will the family. "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Ps 30:5). The morning has not erased the night; both are real, both are remembered, both are held by the same Christ.
webster_summary: A Japanese island prefecture where U.S. Marines are stationed; for the Johns family, the place where three unborn children were lost (2017, 2018) and a personal place of grief and continuing prayer.
webster_full: OKINAWA, place name (personal). The southernmost Japanese island prefecture; major U.S. Marine Corps duty station in the Pacific.

For the editor of this dictionary, the place where his family lost three unborn children during military service: Malachi Andrew (2017), and twin daughters Hope and Mercy (2018). The Johns family's personal "Ramah" / "Bethel-oak-of-weeping."
scriptures: Jeremiah 31:15-17

Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not. Thus saith the LORD; Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy. And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border.
Psalm 30:5
For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Revelation 21:4
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
Genesis 35:8
But Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Bethel under an oak: and the name of it was called Allonbachuth.
corruption_summary: There is no theological corruption to expose for a personal place-name memorial; what may be added is that modern grief-management often encourages "moving on" rather than the biblical practice of REMEMBERING and naming places of loss as part of one's covenant story.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern grief culture often emphasizes "moving on," "closure," or "not dwelling." The Bible takes a different approach. Places of grief are named, marked, and remembered — Bethel's oak is called "oak of weeping" (Allon-bachuth), Rachel's tomb is marked along the way to Bethlehem (Gen 35:19-20), Gilgal preserves the memorial stones of the Jordan crossing (Josh 4:20-24), Ebenezer is named for where the LORD helped (1 Sam 7:12), and Calvary itself is preserved in the Christian memory as the place where the deepest grief became the deepest hope. Christian families who have lost children in specific places are doing biblical work when they name and remember those places.

Okinawa in the Johns family memory is therefore not a wound to be erased but a place to be held — held with the texture of all that has happened there, the sons of grief and the sons of joy intermingled. The morning has come; joy has returned; three living children now bear the family name; the editor's work in this dictionary continues. But the night is also real, and the names of the three little ones lost there — Malachi Andrew, Hope, Mercy — are written here as the Bethel-oak of one Christian family's weeping. The Lord who weeps with His people in Ramah and at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35) holds both the night and the morning.
